content.text: {"primary_meaning": "In mainstream Christian teaching, 'holy' (Hebrew qadosh, Greek hagios) primarily means 'set apart' or 'separated' — designating that which belongs to God and is distinct from the common or profane. Applied to God himself, it denotes his absolute transcendence, otherness, and moral perfection; applied to people, places, and objects, it denotes consecration to God's exclusive use and possession. A tightly connected secondary sense is moral purity: because God is holy, his people are called to ethical purity and separation from sin. Standard teaching thus combines two strands: (1) positional/relational holiness (set apart for God) and (2) moral/ethical holiness (purity of character conforming to God's nature).", "primary_basis": ["Leviticus 19:2 ('Be holy, for I the LORD your God am holy')", "Leviticus 11:44-45", "Isaiah 6:3 ('Holy, holy, holy is the LORD of hosts')", "Exodus 3:5 (holy ground)", "Exodus 19:5-6 ('a kingdom of priests and a holy nation')", "1 Samuel 2:2 ('There is none holy like the LORD')", "1 Peter 1:15-16 ('be holy in all your conduct')", "1 Peter 2:9 ('a holy nation, a people for his own possession')", "Hebrews 12:14 ('the holiness without which no one will see the Lord')", "Revelation 4:8", "Isaiah 57:15", "Psalm 99:1-9"], "alternatives": [{"meaning": "Holiness as primarily moral purity or sinlessness — emphasized in Wesleyan/Holiness traditions (entire sanctification, Christian perfection) where holiness is chiefly an ethical and experiential state produced by the Spirit rather than mainly a positional 'set-apartness.'", "basis": ["1 Thessalonians 4:3-7", "Hebrews 12:14", "Matthew 5:48", "2 Corinthians 7:1", "1 John 3:2-3"], "prominence": "common"}, {"meaning": "Holiness as the numinous — God's awe-inspiring, 'wholly other' transcendence that evokes fear and fascination (Rudolf Otto's 'mysterium tremendum'); holiness is fundamentally God's incomparable divinity rather than an ethical category.", "basis": ["Isaiah 6:1-5", "Exodus 3:5-6", "Exodus 19:16-24", "Job 42:5-6"], "prominence": "common"}, {"meaning": "Holiness as ritual/cultic status within the graded purity system of the Torah — a technical category (holy vs. common, clean vs. unclean) governing sacred space, priesthood, sacrifice, and access to God, as emphasized in biblical scholarship on Leviticus (e.g., Milgrom, Wenham).", "basis": ["Leviticus 10:10", "Leviticus chapters 11-16", "Numbers 4:15", "Ezekiel 44:23", "Haggai 2:11-13"], "prominence": "common"}, {"meaning": "Holiness as positional/definitive sanctification of believers in Christ — 'saints' (hagioi) are holy by union with Christ regardless of attained moral state, with holiness understood as covenantal belonging to God's people.", "basis": ["1 Corinthians 1:2", "1 Corinthians 6:11", "Colossians 3:12", "Ephesians 1:1-4", "Hebrews 10:10"], "prominence": "common"}, {"meaning": "Holiness understood as God's dangerous, contagious power or 'energy' resident in sacred objects and space, which can bless or destroy on contact — a reading found in some history-of-religions and Old Testament scholarship.", "basis": ["2 Samuel 6:6-7 (Uzzah)", "Exodus 19:12-13", "Leviticus 10:1-3", "1 Samuel 6:19-20"], "prominence": "minority"}, {"meaning": "Holiness as essentially identical with God's fullness of being, glory, or love — some theologians (e.g., strands in Barth and in relational theologies) define holiness less as separation and more as God's self-giving otherness expressed in covenant love.", "basis": ["Hosea 11:9 ('the Holy One in your midst')", "Isaiah 57:15", "John 17:17-19"], "prominence": "minority"}], "has_settled_consensus": true, "confidence": "high", "notes": "There is a strong, widely recognized consensus that 'holy' fundamentally means 'set apart / separated unto God,' with God as the ultimate referent and derived holiness for people, places, objects, and times. Virtually all lexicons (BDB, HALOT, TDNT), systematic theologies, and catechetical materials teach this core. The alternatives listed are mostly differences of emphasis (ethical vs. positional vs. cultic vs. numinous) rather than outright rivals; scholars debate whether the etymological sense 'to cut/separate' is primary or whether 'belonging to the divine sphere' is more accurate, but the practical definition in Christian teaching is stable. Any author proposing a materially different symbolic meaning would be departing from a well-settled consensus."}
